articles.title: Abhishek Sharma's 30-ball ton hid the number that should really worry T20 bowlers
articles.summary: The 30-ball ton was, oddly, the least surprising part of what Abhishek Sharma did at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. It isn't even his fastest hundred.
articles.body: The 30-ball ton was, oddly, the least surprising part of what Abhishek Sharma did at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. It isn't even his fastest hundred. What's odd about the innings is what it says about the number sitting next to that extraordinary strike rate: his average.Somewhere in Abhishek Sharma's memory, though, there's a faster century still. It came two years ago, for Punjab against Meghalaya in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy fixture nobody outside domestic cricket was watching: 28 balls, no fanfare.So when he reached three figures in 30 deliveries against Afghanistan in New Delhi, becoming the fastest T20I centurion ever produced by a Full Member nation and only the third-fastest in the format's history overall, it wasn't a discovery. It was a confirmation, delivered on a bigger stage, of something the data had already been saying for a while.The ground has some history with him already. Eight years earlier, on the same square when it was still called Feroz Shah Kotla, a 17-year-old Sharma walked out at number six for Delhi Daredevils against Royal Challengers Bangalore and top-scored on IPL debut — an unbeaten 46 off 19 balls. It was the innings that first put his name into circulation.None of that is really the story, though. The story is what his average has been doing while all this has been going on.The average, not the strike rateAfter 58 T20I innings, Abhishek averages 33.18 at a strike rate of 194.55. Among those who have batted at least 20 times in T20Is since Abhishek's debut in July 2024, nobody has struck as quickly as his 194.55 per 100 balls.Put that alongside the numbers of his closest opening peers and the combination starts to look strange. Phil Salt, across almost the same number of innings, averages 34.34 at 165.89: a fraction higher on average, nearly thirty runs per hundred balls slower. Finn Allen's numbers read 28.67 and 170.74; Travis Head's, 28.40 and 156.69. Multiply strike rate by average and divide by 100 and you get a rough figure for scoring speed without giving up the average: Abhishek comes out at 64.56, against 56.97 for Salt, 48.95 for Allen and 44.50 for Head.The gap isn't really about six-hitting or bravado. It's that T20 cricket generally punishes extreme aggression with a lower average, and in Abhishek's case, over more than fifty innings now, it hasn't.Where the runs actually come fromLook closer and the shape of his batting explains some of it. Of his 1,858 T20I runs, 1,484 (79.9%) have come in boundaries. In the Afghanistan innings that figure spiked to 94.44%, the highest boundary share recorded in any men's T20I century.He hits a six in T20Is every 7.58 balls, comfortably ahead of Allen (8.47), Salt (12.47) and Head (14.20). Zoom out to his whole T20 career, across formats, and he reached his hundredth six faster, by balls faced, than anyone the format has seen, edging West Indies' Evin Lewis. Among Indian batters with 50 or more T20 sixes, nobody has matched his rate of clearing the boundary. He's the best of the lot, streets ahead of Sanju Samson, Shivam Dube, Suryakumar Yadav and Yuvraj Singh, the mentor whose fastest-fifty record he's now threatened on at least three occasions.The first six oversThe clearest expression of the method is the powerplay. His strike rate in an innings' first ten balls, 176, is the joint-highest on record, level with Tim David: he isn't feeling out the pitch before he attacks. His boundary percentage inside the powerplay, 33.48% according to CricViz, is the best among batters with 500-plus T20I runs.This has happened before, too. India have breached 90 in a T20I powerplay four times, and Abhishek has been the one doing the damage on every occasion: 59 not out off 21 against England at the Wankhede last year, 51 not out off 14 against New Zealand in Guwahati this year, 51 off 19 in the World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where he reached fifty in 18 balls under the most pressure he's likely ever faced. His 76 not out off 22 balls is simply the largest number yet on that list. His opening stand with Samson, 142 off 59 balls, is now the fastest century opening partnership for India in T20Is by run rate, overtaking a stand between KL Rahul and Rohit Sharma from Indore in 2017.What it costs himNone of this comes free. Abhishek walked into this year's T20 World Cup and made three consecutive ducks, followed that with 15, 10 and 9, and salvaged the campaign with two match-defining fifties, one in a must-win Super Eight game against Zimbabwe, the other in the final. Eight innings, 141 runs, an average of 17.62. "As a batter, as a cricketer, sometimes [my form is] going to go up and down," he said afterwards, and there's little sense he sees the ducks as a separate problem from the sixes. They're the same bet, landing differently.And 2026 has underlined that cost. Abhishek has been dismissed for a duck 10 times in T20 cricket this calendar year, the most by any batter in a year, ahead of Rashid Khan's nine in 2019 and Shadab Khan's nine in 2024. Five of those have come off the first ball, making him the joint-most prolific first-ball duck-maker in a calendar year in T20Is, alongside Rwanda's Kevin Irakoze in 2023 and Richard Ngarava in 2024.What's changed isn't the risk-taking. It's how deliberately he manages it. Against the Rashid Khan, Mohammad Nabi and Mujeeb Ur Rahman spin trio in the Afghanistan series, he made a conscious tactical switch, going only forward or down the pitch, never back, and scored 54 off 15 against them, including 4, 4, 6 off three straight Rashid deliveries in the last over of the powerplay.In the first two games, camped on the back foot against the same bowlers, he'd managed only 29 off 17. "It's always about me backing my shots because I don't have a lot of shots," he said earlier this year, after an 85 off 34 against New Zealand, which sounds like modesty until you notice how precisely that limited toolkit is being aimed.Level with KohliThis is now his tenth century in all forms of T20 cricket, level with Virat Kohli for the most by an Indian batter, and his third T20I hundred, level with Samson, and behind only Rohit Sharma and Suryakumar Yadav in India's own list. The number worth sitting with isn't the 30 balls. It came with a string of milestones and records as the India star continued to show his ability to score quickly even at this stage of his career.Kohli hit 139 not out off 88 balls in India's eight-wicket win in Thiruvananthapuram. His century came off 74 balls, making it the third-fastest ODI hundred of his career.Kohli's fastest ODI hundredsKohli's fastest ODI century remains his 52-ball hundred against Australia in Jaipur in 2013. He followed it with a 61-ball hundred against Australia in Nagpur later that year.His latest 74-ball century moved into third place. His next three fastest hundreds came off 76, 76 and 80 balls, against Sri Lanka in Hobart, Colombo and Guwahati respectively.Virat Kohli's fastest ODI centuries52 balls vs Australia, Jaipur, 201361 balls vs Australia, Nagpur, 201374 balls vs West Indies, Thiruvananthapuram, 202676 balls vs Sri Lanka, Hobart, 201276 balls vs Sri Lanka, Colombo RPS, 201780 balls vs Sri Lanka, Guwahati, 2023Another 10-century record for KohliThe century was also Kohli's 10th ODI hundred against West Indies. He already had 10 ODI centuries against Sri Lanka. That made Kohli the only batter in ODI history with 10 centuries against two different teams.Most ODI centuries against a team:10 - Virat Kohli vs Sri Lanka10 - Virat Kohli vs West Indies9 - Sachin Tendulkar vs Australia9 - Rohit Sharma vs Australia8 - Virat Kohli vs Australia8 - Sachin Tendulkar vs Sri LankaKohli matches Tendulkar's List A recordKohli's century also took his List A hundred tally to 60, putting him level with Sachin Tendulkar at the top of the list. Tendulkar reached 60 List A centuries in 538 innings, while Kohli got there in 338 innings.Kohli's other records from the inningsKohli's 139 not out also included nine sixes, his most in an ODI innings. His previous best was eight sixes against Sri Lanka in Thiruvananthapuram in 2023. He also scored 53 runs off Alzarri Joseph, his most against the bowler in an ODI.Kohli has now been involved in 112 ODI wins while chasing, with only Sachin Tendulkar and MS Dhoni ahead of him on the list.Involved in most wins in ODI run chases127 S Tendulkar116 MS Dhoni112 V Kohli111 R Ponting110 J Kallis/ Rohit SharmaMost runs by Kohli off a bowler in an ODI54 vs Trent Boult Mohali 201653 vs Alzarri Jospeh Trivandrum 202645 vs Vishwa Fernando Colombo RPS 201745 vs Lahiru Kumara Trivandrum 202345 vs Prenalen Subrayen Ranchi 2025Most sixes by Kohli in an ODI innings9 vs WI Trivandrum 2026 *8 vs SL Trivandrum 20237 vs Aus Jaipur 20137 vs SA Ranchi 2025Kohli wants to keep playing positivelyKohli said playing only one format for India has given him clarity, with the 2027 World Cup now a clear target."Well, thank you firstly for the kind words. Well, my focus has never really been on these milestones, so to say. It's just understanding the situation along the course of just doing the job for the team, whatever. Achievements come along," Kohli said after the match."Obviously, I feel very grateful and very blessed to be in this position for having played for so long. articles.title: Asian Games: Rain threatens Shreyas Iyer-led India’s title defence ahead of Afghanistan quarterfinal
articles.summary: Nisshin: Even if a single ball is not bowled, the Indian men’s cricket team will still retain the Asian Games gold they won in the previous edition on
articles.body: Nisshin: Even if a single ball is not bowled, the Indian men’s cricket team will still retain the Asian Games gold they won in the previous edition on debut. Going by the weather here, the situation cannot be ruled out. The only constant for the Indian team from the time they landed in Tokyo a week ago has been rain. Apart from a couple of indoor net sessions, the players have probably held an umbrella more than a bat or a ball.They arrived in Nagoya with a steady drizzle on Saturday afternoon and their practice session on Sunday was halted midway due to rain again. With the venue being a makeshift cricket stadium, there were no indoor facilities for the team to turn to.But skipper Shreyas Iyer refused to dwell on the weather conditions. “There is rain, but we can’t use that as an excuse. Such hurdles will keep coming. Irrespective of the situation, we are mentally prepared (to play). We got a decent warm-up and a little practice (before the rain). We will try to adapt as soon as possible to the wicket.” In the quarterfinals on Monday, they face Afghanistan.At the Korogi Sports Park here, Afghanistan come into the contest on the back of a mixed campaign so far. While they had an easy outing against hosts Japan in their campaign opener, they were handed a five-wicket loss by Nepal on Friday.The results are the outcome of the fact that Afghanistan is fielding a second-string team in the tournament with skipper Darwish Rasooli and Abdollah Ahmadzai, the only players in the squad from the team which lost to India 0-3 in a bilateral series recently.A full-strength Indian team against a rookie Afghanistan side may seem like a contest of the uneven, but the Indian team will know better than taking the Afghans lightly, especially after their near-loss. In the five-over rain-truncated contest India managed 32/4 and then scrapped through with a two-run margin.“We can’t take any team in the Asian Games lightly because the wicket here cannot be set to a particular standard. It will be challenging and difficult for every team.”Iyer also cited the example of the recent match against Japan, a rain-truncated contest. It will be interesting to see if India will risk playing Jasprit Bumrah, who was rested for the match against Japan, given he is coming back from injury and the outfield may not be the best.While the stage is set for the title defence, one can only hope for th srain to stay away, especially for the scores of Indian fans, who are planning to travel from across Japan to root for the men in blue.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Abhishek Sharma's 30-ball ton hid the number that should really worry T20 bowlers
articles.summary: Abhishek Sharma's 30-ball T20I hundred against Afghanistan was spectacular, but the bigger story lies in the numbers around it. The India opener is striking...
articles.body:
The 30-ball ton was, oddly, the least surprising part of what Abhishek Sharma did at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. It isn't even his fastest hundred. What's odd about the innings is what it says about the number sitting next to that extraordinary strike rate: his average. Somewhere in Abhishek Sharma's memory, though, there's a faster century still. It came two years ago, for Punjab against Meghalaya in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy fixture nobody outside domestic cricket was watching: 28 balls, no fanfare. So when he reached three figures in 30 deliveries against Afghanistan in New Delhi, becoming the fastest T20I centurion ever produced by a Full Member nation and only the third-fastest in the format's history overall, it wasn't a discovery. It was a confirmation, delivered on a bigger stage, of something the data had already been saying for a while.

The ground has some history with him already. Eight years earlier, on the same square when it was still called Feroz Shah Kotla, a 17-year-old Sharma walked out at number six for Delhi Daredevils against Royal Challengers Bangalore and top-scored on IPL debut — an unbeaten 46 off 19 balls. It was the innings that first put his name into circulation. None of that is really the story, though. The story is what his average has been doing while all this has been going on. The average, not the strike rate After 58 T20I innings, Abhishek averages 33.18 at a strike rate of 194.55. Among those who have batted at least 20 times in T20Is since Abhishek's debut in July 2024, nobody has struck as quickly as his 194.55 per 100 balls.

Put that alongside the numbers of his closest opening peers and the combination starts to look strange. Phil Salt, across almost the same number of innings, averages 34.34 at 165.89: a fraction higher on average, nearly thirty runs per hundred balls slower. Finn Allen's numbers read 28.67 and 170.74; Travis Head's, 28.40 and 156.69. Multiply strike rate by average and divide by 100 and you get a rough figure for scoring speed without giving up the average: Abhishek comes out at 64.56, against 56.97 for Salt, 48.95 for Allen and 44.50 for Head. The gap isn't really about six-hitting or bravado. It's that T20 cricket generally punishes extreme aggression with a lower average, and in Abhishek's case, over more than fifty innings now, it hasn't. Where the runs actually come from Look closer and the shape of his batting explains some of it. Of his 1,858 T20I runs, 1,484 (79.9%) have come in boundaries. In the Afghanistan innings that figure spiked to 94.44%, the highest boundary share recorded in any men's T20I century.

He hits a six in T20Is every 7.58 balls, comfortably ahead of Allen (8.47), Salt (12.47) and Head (14.20). Zoom out to his whole T20 career, across formats, and he reached his hundredth six faster, by balls faced, than anyone the format has seen, edging West Indies' Evin Lewis. Among Indian batters with 50 or more T20 sixes, nobody has matched his rate of clearing the boundary. He's the best of the lot, streets ahead of Sanju Samson, Shivam Dube, Suryakumar Yadav and Yuvraj Singh, the mentor whose fastest-fifty record he's now threatened on at least three occasions.

The first six overs The clearest expression of the method is the powerplay. His strike rate in an innings' first ten balls, 176, is the joint-highest on record, level with Tim David: he isn't feeling out the pitch before he attacks. His boundary percentage inside the powerplay, 33.48% according to CricViz, is the best among batters with 500-plus T20I runs.

This has happened before, too. India have breached 90 in a T20I powerplay four times, and Abhishek has been the one doing the damage on every occasion: 59 not out off 21 against England at the Wankhede last year, 51 not out off 14 against New Zealand in Guwahati this year, 51 off 19 in the World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where he reached fifty in 18 balls under the most pressure he's likely ever faced. His 76 not out off 22 balls is simply the largest number yet on that list. His opening stand with Samson, 142 off 59 balls, is now the fastest century opening partnership for India in T20Is by run rate, overtaking a stand between KL Rahul and Rohit Sharma from Indore in 2017. What it costs him None of this comes free. Abhishek walked into this year's T20 World Cup and made three consecutive ducks, followed that with 15, 10 and 9, and salvaged the campaign with two match-defining fifties, one in a must-win Super Eight game against Zimbabwe, the other in the final. Eight innings, 141 runs, an average of 17.62. "As a batter, as a cricketer, sometimes [my form is] going to go up and down," he said afterwards, and there's little sense he sees the ducks as a separate problem from the sixes. They're the same bet, landing differently.

And 2026 has underlined that cost. Abhishek has been dismissed for a duck 10 times in T20 cricket this calendar year, the most by any batter in a year, ahead of Rashid Khan's nine in 2019 and Shadab Khan's nine in 2024. Five of those have come off the first ball, making him the joint-most prolific first-ball duck-maker in a calendar year in T20Is, alongside Rwanda's Kevin Irakoze in 2023 and Richard Ngarava in 2024. What's changed isn't the risk-taking. It's how deliberately he manages it. Against the Rashid Khan, Mohammad Nabi and Mujeeb Ur Rahman spin trio in the Afghanistan series, he made a conscious tactical switch, going only forward or down the pitch, never back, and scored 54 off 15 against them, including 4, 4, 6 off three straight Rashid deliveries in the last over of the powerplay. In the first two games, camped on the back foot against the same bowlers, he'd managed only 29 off 17. "It's always about me backing my shots because I don't have a lot of shots," he said earlier this year, after an 85 off 34 against New Zealand, which sounds like modesty until you notice how precisely that limited toolkit is being aimed. Level with Kohli

This is now his tenth century in all forms of T20 cricket, level with Virat Kohli for the most by an Indian batter, and his third T20I hundred, level with Samson, and behind only Rohit Sharma and Suryakumar Yadav in India's own list. The number worth sitting with isn't the 30 balls. It's how Abhishek has managed to keep his average above 30 while scoring at a strike rate of nearly 195.

articles.title: Defending Champions India through to Asian Games semi-final as rain washes out quarter-final against Afghanistan
articles.summary: India’s men’s cricket team advanced to the semi-finals of the 2026 Asian Games without taking the field after persistent rain forced their quarter-final
articles.body: India’s men’s cricket team advanced to the semi-finals of the 2026 Asian Games without taking the field after persistent rain forced their quarter-final against Afghanistan to be abandoned in Nisshin, Japan.With dark clouds and steady rain keeping the covers firmly in place and conditions showing no signs of improving, the match was eventually called off without a ball being bowled, sending India through to the last four under the tournament’s knockout rules.India will now face the winner of the Sri Lanka-Nepal quarter-final in the semi-finals as they continue their bid to retain the gold medal they won at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.Iyer leads strong Indian squadIndia entered the tournament with a strong squad featuring several established international names. Shreyas Iyer is leading the side, with Tilak Varma serving as his deputy.The squad includes Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Shivam Dube, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Varun Chakaravarthy, Ravi Bishnoi, Jasprit Bumrah, Arshdeep Singh, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Yash Thakur.Former India cricketer VVS Laxman is serving as the team’s stand-in head coach for the Asian Games campaign.India eye back-to-back Asian Games goldIndia are aiming to retain the men’s cricket gold medal they won at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Their campaign in the previous edition also ended with a weather-affected final, with India awarded the gold medal after their title clash against Afghanistan was washed out.The Indian women’s team has already successfully defended its Asian Games title in Aichi-Nagoya. Harmanpreet Kaur-led India defeated Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final to claim the gold medal.Pakistan also through after washoutEarlier, Pakistan also advanced to the men’s semi-finals after their quarter-final against Hong Kong, China was abandoned due to rain. articles.title: England cricket: Brendon McCullum proposes 50-over warm-ups - how are side shaping up for World Cup?
articles.summary: Who are England's openers? Which spinner supports Adil Rashid? Which seamers will get the nod when Sam Curran returns?
articles.body:
The most surprising moment of England's thumping win over Sri Lanka at The Oval was not Jofra Archer's direct hit run-out, nor Tom Banton's first international century.

It came in an answer that coach Brendon McCullum gave afterwards.

"We are also trying to include a number of warm-up games as well," McCullum told BBC Test Match Special of his winter plans.

That is McCullum, the coach whose side had only one in-house warm-up before last winter's Ashes, talking about arranging 50-over practice matches - something England have not had on a tour outside World Cups for six years in the longest white-ball format.

"A lot of these guys just haven't played a lot of white-ball cricket," McCullum said.

It was an eyebrow-raising, yet encouraging, answer which hints at a change in McCullum, who has also had a beefed-up backroom staff this summer and spoke on more than one occasion about fitness in the Oval aftermath.

And a team that lost six of seven ODI series between their final match of a dismal 2023 World Cup and the end of last year - exiting the Champions Trophy without winning a game in between - have won all three of their 50-over series this year.

With the next World Cup a year away, England may not be the best 50-over side in the world, but they are no longer the format's biggest underachievers.

"I think they might be in with a shout, with a bit of luck on their side," said former England spinner Phil Tufnell.

There is hope again, albeit with some issues to solve…

England win series as Banton delivers on potential

In the most bizarre of cricketing summers, Ben Duckett has had a bizarre summer of his own.

The only Englishman to compile a Test ton, and the scorer of 141 against India in a one-day international at Lord's, ends with nine scores below 20 from his other 15 innings.

He was talked about as the world's best all-format batter after his 149 against India last summer but has averaged 27.15 since then across formats.

It is right that England are reticent to drop a batter who has hit such highs, especially as a senior player and one with significant List A experience - a total of 111 matches - behind him in a squad still lacking in 50-over matches.

Duckett and Jacob Bethell also shared an opening stand of 192 in the series decider against India at Lord's.

But, unlike the Test side where Emilio Gay's place as Duckett's partner is not fully secure, never mind a replacement waiting in the wings, Tom Banton and Bethell have shown there could be another world without the diminutive left-hander.

Bethell, who scored 91 in the third ODI against India before missing the Sri Lanka series with a knee injury, is talked of as a senior player in the group, despite still being just 22, while Banton's first England century on Sunday was superb.

The way Banton hits the ball at the top of the bounce looks suited to the bouncy pitches of South Africa, where the majority of the World Cup will be played.

Duckett, in contrast, averages 23.4 on surfaces deemed as 'high bouncing' since the start of 2023. This winter's Test series in South Africa may shed some more light.

This was supposed to be the series Rehan Ahmed got his long-awaited chance as England's leg-spinner with Adil Rashid injured. That the 22-year-old was dropped for the series decider is of obvious concern.

Ahmed bowled better than figures of 1-46 suggested in the first ODI, but was flattered by a return of 2-48 from eight overs in the second.

In his place at The Oval, Liam Dawson - 14 years his senior - took 3-26.

Dawson was helped by the combination of turn and bounce on offer from the surface, something Ahmed was not afforded earlier in the series.

But he also landed 39% of deliveries on a spinner's 'good' length, compared to the 22% from Ahmed in the previous two games.

Ahmed is clearly talented but has not progressed as an international cricketer. A sloppy run-out in Durham and a five-ball duck in the Headingley chase did not help his cause.

It leaves Rashid, who will be 39 at the World Cup, as important as ever.

While the alarming statistics that England have won only one of their past nine ODIs in which neither captain Harry Brook nor number three Joe Root made fifty remains, Sunday's win was significant given the key contributions from other names.

Banton laid the platform of their 355-7 and Jordan Cox's 52-ball 76 pushed the game beyond Sri Lanka.

Cox's opportunity came after an injury to Jos Buttler in the second ODI. The way he took down the Sri Lanka bowling was an ideal imitation of England's greatest white-ball player.

Buttler is facing a spell on the sidelines with his hamstring injury but on this evidence England have a capable understudy. Again, experience will come into the equation if Cox's form suggests a more drastic decision must be made.

Buttler's brilliant boundary-hitting before being cut down by injury in the second ODI showed his best days are not necessarily all behind him. Equally, the 36-year-old's injury reminded no-one can go on forever.

With Cox having made a breakout summer across formats and Banton likely to get more opportunities before Bethell returns, England are beginning to build promising depth.

The impending return of Sam Curran from a groin injury - who remains important as a left-handed batter and seam-bowling option in the top seven - could also create a squeeze for places.

At his best, the all-rounder would improve the balance which was slightly bowling-heavy in this series but would likely leave England needing to leave out two of Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Jamie Overton, Josh Tongue and Sonny Baker from their first-choice XI.

Despite a quiet series at the end of a long summer, Archer remains England's trump card. Atkinson has been the most accurate - 49% of his powerplay deliveries have hit a good length - and economical new-ball bowler, while Overton appears to have been given the middle-over enforcer role.

Most intriguing was Baker's opening spell at The Oval.

McCullum said he was brought in to provide some new-ball "X-Factor", with only Atkinson (five) having taken more than one wicket in the powerplay across England's ODIs this summer.

With a swinging, rising delivery that nicked off Pathum Nissanka, Baker took his first with his second delivery and, albeit after only two ODIs, is one of only five bowlers to average more than 85mph and over one degree of swing inside the powerplay in the format.

India's Mohammed Siraj and Mohammed Shami, West Indies Alzarri Joseph and Australia's Mitchell Starc are the others.

He is a wildcard England must consider when completing the jigsaw over the 20-or-so ODIs before the World Cup begins.

articles.title: Jos Buttler: England wicketkeeper ruled out of tri-series in Pakistan with injury
articles.summary: Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler will miss England's 50-over tri-series in Pakistan next month, with Jordan Cox set to be given another chance to impress in his place.
articles.body:
Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler will miss England's 50-over tri-series in Pakistan next month, with Jordan Cox set to be given another chance to impress in his place.

Coach Brendon McCullum said it is "hard to judge" how long Buttler will be out for and confirmed Cox will take his place for the series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka, which begins on 20 October.

"We know Jos is an incredible athlete, we know he is supremely fit and is an ultra-professional," McCullum said.

"He will do everything he can to be back as soon as possible."

England also tour Australia for white-ball matches in November - where they are considering playing warm-up matches - as they look to add to their six series wins in limited-overs cricket this year and build towards next year's 50-over World Cup.

They will finalise their squads on Monday with the latest batch of central contracts also set to be announced in the coming days.

Durham opener Emilio Gay is in line for a first deal after his debut Test summer, putting him in line to tour South Africa this winter, while Cox, Tom Banton, who scored his first international century on Sunday , and all-rounder Dan Lawrence could also feature.

Contracts held by former captain Ben Stokes and Mark Wood are set to end after their international retirements. Ollie Pope, Zak Crawley, Matthew Potts and Luke Wood are all out of favour and their one-year deals are due to run out.

Spinner Shoaib Bashir is another intriguing name in that category. He played two Tests against New Zealand and was picked in the Test squad to play Pakistan but did not make an XI as England preferred a four-man pace attack.

England are learning - these are the World Cup issues they need to solve

In a breakout international summer, Cox impressed by scoring fifties in all three Tests when picked to bat number three against Pakistan. He also hit 76 against Sri Lanka when deputising for Buttler in the third ODI at The Oval on Sunday.

"I thought it was quite a Jos Buttler innings," McCullum said.

"He has done really well domestically for a number of years and has been unlucky with injuries.

"For him to have the type of summer he has had and be in the position he is in, he deserves it.

"He is a phenomenal talent, is very well liked in dressing room as well and seems to be one of those guys who is good at everything he does, which will be incredibly annoying."

England will also make a decision on whether to pick bowler Brydon Carse to tour Pakistan. He has not been selected since being arrested then de-arrested on a night out in Derby in August.

After a police investigation ended without action, he is now subject to a Cricket Regulator investigation and, while he remains available for selection, white-ball captain Harry Brook said last week he needs time away from the international scene .

McCullum, who began the summer as England's coach across the three formats before being sacked from the Test role in July, dismissed any suggestion of regret at the end of the English season.

"I loved coaching all three formats," he said. "Things move on, times change. I am biased but I genuinely think [new Test coach] Stephen Fleming will do an unbelievable job with the red-ball side.

"With the extra bit of time it probably does allow you to drill down on a few aspects you have identified you need to improve or shape things differently to get to where you want to."

There will be Test Match Special commentary on England's white-ball tours to Pakistan and Australia this autumn

articles.title: England batter Jos Buttler ruled out of Pakistan white-ball tour after injury in second ODI against Sri Lanka
articles.summary: Jos Buttler will miss England's white-ball tour of Pakistan after suffering an injury against Sri Lanka in the second ODI at Headingley; Tom Banton opened the batting in the third ODI on Sunday, making 126 off 105 balls in his absence; Jordan Cox expected to keep wicket
articles.body:
Buttler injured his hamstring during his innings against Sri Lanka at Headingley last week, initially retiring hurt before returning to the crease later on despite being visibly hampered by the injury.

He sat out Sunday's series decider at the Kia Oval , which England won comfortably by 223 runs, and has now been ruled out of next month's 50-over tri-series.

That leaves England without arguably their most accomplished white-ball player as they look to build a side capable of challenging for silverware in southern Africa next winter, with no guarantee yet that the 36-year-old will be fit to return for the subsequent tour of Australia in November.

"Jos won't be in Pakistan," limited-overs coach Brendon McCullum confirmed.

"We know he's an incredible athlete, we know he's supremely fit and an ultra-professional, so he'll do everything he can to get back as soon as possible, but it's hard to judge how long that will be.

"It's disappointing not to have Jos but it will be good for us to see where we're at. Between now and 14 months' time lots of things will go wrong, there'll be lots of selections you think will happen and someone will get injured, or there'll be a scheduling issue.

"You almost have to catastrophise these things a little to prepare yourself for that World Cup."

Buttler injury hands opportunity to in-form Cox

In the short term, that means an extended opportunity for Jordan Cox as the wicketkeeper-batter. He returned to the ODI side for the first time in nearly two years against Sri Lanka and capped an impressive summer by steering England through the death overs with a fluent 76.

"I thought that was quite a Jos Buttler innings," said McCullum.

"Cox will definitely get the opportunity in Pakistan. He's done really well domestically for a number of years and he's been unlucky with injuries when he's been on the cusp previously.

"He's deserved it. He's very well liked in our dressing room and he seems to be one of those guys who is good at whatever he does, which can be incredibly annoying.

"He's a good lad with a huge amount of runway in front of him in his career."

England are set to finalise their squad for Pakistan within the next 24 hours, with Sam Curran pushing for a return after a groin problem and further checks to be carried out on Adil Rashid's bowling hand. Jacob Bethell, meanwhile, is still recovering from a knee injury.

For McCullum, there is now a short break after a rollercoaster summer. Having retained his position as England's all-format head coach following a difficult Ashes campaign, he showed a willingness to adapt his methods, bolstering his backroom staff and taking a more rigorous approach to training.

He was subsequently removed from the Test role following Ben Stokes' retirement and the series defeat by New Zealand, but enters the winter programme in charge of an improving white-ball side that has won 11 of its last 13 matches.

McCullum's latest challenge is to turn England into "the fittest, fastest, most dynamic and robust cricket team out there", while he has also outlined plans to bolster the touring schedule with additional warm-up matches after scrapping such fixtures during his early days in charge of the red-ball side.

Reflecting on a season of change and looking ahead to his split coaching partnership with new Test head coach Stephen Fleming, McCullum said: "It's been eventful. I genuinely feel right now, at the end of the summer, English cricket is certainly in a really good place.

"I loved coaching all three formats. The four years I had as Test coach were one of the most enjoyable periods of my time in cricket. But things move on, times change. I think Stephen [Fleming] will do an unbelievable job with the Test side.

"Overall, it's no bad thing that it sits the way it sits now."

articles.title: Somerset rue dropped points as County Championship title slips away again
articles.summary: Somerset senior figures lament a lack of ruthlessness earlier in the season as team settle for another second place in the County Championship.
articles.body:
A few weeks ago Somerset fans might have been daring to dream that 2026 would finally be the year their team would turn from nearly men into County Championship winners.

With two games to go, Somerset were top of the table by four points. Destiny was in their hands as they sought to win their first-ever Championship trophy.

But a second defeat of the season at the hands of Yorkshire , this time at Headingley, in their penultimate game was like a sledgehammer to the heart of fans and meant Somerset handed over control to eventual winners Warwickshire to clinch glory in the final match on Saturday.

Somerset stay as cricket's perennial runners-up for another 12 months, with this their sixth second-place finish in the Championship since 2010 as they remain one of just three counties to never lift the trophy.

While the Yorkshire defeat on 18 September sealed their fate, senior figures in the club pointed instead to a lack of ruthlessness earlier in the campaign when citing the moments where the trophy slipped through their fingers.

"Two weeks ago we were in a great place to win the thing that we've been trying hard to do for a very long time," captain Lewis Gregory told BBC Radio Somerset.

"But it's probably a couple of games in the middle of the year that are the defining moments.

"There were two games we were in a really good spot - probably didn't show the ruthlessness that we needed, to put us in a position where we were the only team that could win."

The Bears' necessity: Just how good is top wicket-taker Bamber?

Somerset director of cricket Andy Hurry echoed Gregory's assessment and pointed specifically to the back-to-back defeats by Yorkshire in Taunton and Glamorgan in Cardiff in May.

Yorkshire overturned a 112-run first-innings deficit to beat Somerset by 75 runs, while Glamorgan achieved a shock win by just two wickets - their first victory at home in Division One.

"There's been a number of games which we should have won, we didn't get the outcome we were looking for," Hurry told BBC 5 Live, hours before Warwickshire were confirmed as champions.

"Glamorgan were incredible over in Cardiff, the resilience they showed. We put all the effort in and didn't quite get the rub of the green.

"The game here [in Taunton] against Yorkshire was another important game for us and again not quite getting that result.

"So how do we convert those games from the outcome we got this year into positive results moving forward - that's going to be a big focus for us."

Gregory said while there was a "lot of disappointment" within the squad, players would only improve from the experiences this year.

"We've got some amazingly talented cricketers in the squad and there's a lot of guys that will be better for the experience of of this year and hopefully kick on even more," he said.

Hurry too was confident the team's trajectory overall in 2026 was trending upwards, pointing to improvements in both the batting and bowling units.

"We can't get it across the line this year there's been a tremendous effort by so many people - the bowling unit have been phenomenal this year and it's been really encouraging to also see the contributions from the top six as well," Hurry said.

"There's been some real growth in how we're approaching our cricket at the moment and it's very exciting for the future of Somerset."

However, Hurry added: "But we want to win trophies and we want to win them consistently and that's really really important to us."

articles.title: The clear priorities England must tackle after turbulent summer
articles.summary: IN DEPTH: The England men’s side must settle on new central contracts and find balance in selection across three formats, writes Harry Latham-Coyle, with opp...
articles.body:
At the end of a chaotic couple of months, there was one last piece of Brendon McCullum understatement to part with as the curtain came down. "It's been eventful," England's white-ball coach remarked of a strange summer that may be remembered more for the wrong reasons than the right ones.

But McCullum's next comment required slightly more scrutiny. "I genuinely feel right now, at the end of the summer, English cricket is certainly in a really good place," he opined, obviously with a vested interest as an individual who began the summer as their men's all-format supremo and closed it adjusting to life working again alongside good chum Stephen Fleming . Could it really be said that out of the tumult that characterised so much of the cricketing year, England have emerged better and brighter than before? Certainly, that argument can be made.

In terms of pure accounting, the overall win-loss record is encouraging: in red-ball cricket, played six, lost two; in coloured clothing, a rise to No 1 in the world in the T20 format and two strong series wins in 50-over cricket represent signs of real progress. In McCullum and Harry Brook , and Fleming and Joe Root , England appear to have two distinct sets of leaders with their own defined identities but immense comfort working with one another – while they may reflect that Pakistan and Sri Lanka, latterly, were not perhaps top-class tourists, there is at least a foundation from which to rebuild after England rather burned the house down in the Tests against New Zealand.

As reflected upon before, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) erred in backing McCullum and Ben Stokes so strongly after the Ashes, squandering time and a Test series when all could see a fresh start was required. Rob Key and co. would argue – with some justification – that making a change earlier would have meant missing out on Stephen Fleming, inadvertently an ideal fit for the curious circumstances under which he will assume duties as Test head coach. To come out with a relatively positive overall record and sense of optimism about all three sides given how things appeared to veer off the rails either side of the retirement of Stokes will leave the hierarchy relatively pleased.

The all-rounder's departure meant the side losing another of its big beasts that have characterised the last decade; only Root and Jos Buttler , who will miss the tour of Pakistan next month as he recovers from his hamstring injury, remain. It is encouraging, then, that others have begun to assume and enjoy fresh prominence. Brook has proved a shrewd leader in white-ball cricket and has looked a class apart at times with the bat, while the careful management of Jofra Archer has paid dividends in an injury-free and impactful summer. In he, Ollie Robinson , Josh Tongue , Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker, there is a fast-bowling stable of variety and venom – though tougher tests on less friendly pitches in red-ball cricket await.

A refreshing of central contracts is due in the coming days, which, as ever, will be instructive. Emilio Gay is thought likely to receive a first deal, which would indicate the likelihood of touring South Africa even with his place far from certain . Jordan Cox, by contrast, feels to have seized his chance to become an all-format regular. "I thought that was quite a Jos Buttler innings," said McCullum of the Essex batter's 76 in the third ODI against Sri Lanka. "He's done really well domestically for a number of years and he's been unlucky with injuries when he's been on the cusp previously. He's deserved it. He's very well liked in our dressing room and he seems to be one of those guys who is good at whatever he does, which can be incredibly annoying."

Dan Lawrence , too, seems to have swelled in stature within the environment as another adaptable, attacking cricketer. His place as lead spinner in the Test team remains a bit of a bodge but England are not replete with proven alternative options. It has been a tough week or so for Rehan Ahmed in the absence of an injured Adil Rashid , with the leggie left out at the Oval after two middling ODI outings with ball and bat. Rashid will be 39 come next year's World Cup and remains as important as ever; Liam Dawson is two years his junior and now free to whittle away with his white-ball wiles having given up red-ball cricket. To see South Africa bowl 30 overs of finger-spin in their second ODI win over Australia in Johannesburg showed that balance will be necessary come the tournament in just over a year's time.

Having found a winning formula, the Test team are less likely to tinker with their four seam spearheads when they arrive in the nation rather sooner. They will surely take an alternative spin option – Shoaib Bashir may be feeling vulnerable about his central contract – in December with half an eye on Tests in Bangladesh two months later. It is a curious itinerary ahead for Fleming to plot through – after that short sojourn comes one shorter still for the 150th Anniversary Test at the MCG, before Bangladesh visit for a one-off encounter at Lord's. That should at least leave his side well prepared for the Ashes; to hear McCullum demand an expanded programme of warm-up games ahead of the World Cup suggested at least one lesson had been learned from the missteps of the reverse encounter Down Under. England remain a work in progress but there is at least work and progress of which to speak.

articles.summary: MUMBAI: In a major boost to Mumbai ahead of the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season, opener Ayush Mhatre, out of action since he suffered a bad hamstring injury
articles.body: MUMBAI: In a major boost to Mumbai ahead of the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season, opener Ayush Mhatre, out of action since he suffered a bad hamstring injury while playing for the Chennai Super Kings during IPL-2026, will play his first competitive match in almost five months when he will turn out in a practice match amongst Mumbai's Ranji Trophy probables at the Cricket Club of India on Tuesday."Ayush is now completely fit and has recovered from his injuries in both the hamstrings. articles.title: Ed Joyce: Former international appointed Ireland men's batting coach
articles.summary: Cricket Ireland name former international Ed Joyce as the new High Performance batting coach, with a focus on the the men's senior squad and male talent pathway.
articles.body:
Cricket Ireland has named former international Ed Joyce as its new high performance batting coach, with a focus on the the men's senior squad and male talent pathway.

Joyce played 151 times for Ireland, scoring 5,552 runs at an average of 40.82 with 10 centuries and 29 half-centuries.

In 2019, one year after his playing retirement, Joyce became head coach of Ireland women and stayed in the role until stepping down last year.

"The head coach role with Ireland women was a great experience and I enjoyed the day-to-day aspect of working with players on developing and improving their techniques and mindset," he said.

"Despite the power game coming to the fore, having a sound technique and a positive mindset are still crucial aspects for any batter at this level.

"When I look at the Ireland men's side over recent years, it's obvious to see the amount of hard work that has gone on behind the scenes in preparing our players to be competitive on the international stage.

"I look forward to getting involved in this work and perhaps adding some insights and knowledge to push the batting group forward. The talent is there, the goal is now consistency."

Joyce also played for England on 19 occasions.

articles.title: Leicestershire: Eight-point penalty removed but appeal process remains ongoing
articles.summary: Leicestershire have eight points of their 27-point County Championship deduction reinstated but their Division One status remains in limbo.
articles.body:
Leicestershire have had eight points of their 27-point County Championship deduction reinstated but their Division One status remains in limbo.

The original penalty for breaching pitch regulations, relating to their win against Glamorgan in August, was announced on 16 September.

The amendment to the punishment comes after the Cricket Regulator raised with the Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) whether the 19-point penalty imposed under the County Championship's playing conditions had been taken into account when making its original decision.

The Cricket Regulator said it had "raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC in the interests of fairness and transparency".

A section of the County Championship's playing conditions state that teams charged with producing a pitch rated as poor or below average, and the CDP upholding the charge, would receive zero points from the fixture in question.

Leicestershire took 19 points from the match against Glamorgan - 16 for winning and three bonus points - which were removed but remain the subject of appeal.

The CDP had applied an additional eight-point deduction, a further eight-point penalty suspended for a year, plus a £5,000 fine.

The latter two sanctions remain part of the amended decision but the eight-point deduction for this season has been waived.

Without the 27 points being docked, Leicestershire would have finished two points above the relegation zone.

After the eight-point reinstatement but with the 19-point penalty still in place, the Foxes are 17 points behind Essex and will be relegated if their appeal is unsuccessful.

Leicestershire had already stated their intention to appeal against the panel's decision and a statement by chief executive Emma White said the club's position is "unchanged" by the amendment.

Leicestershire to appeal against 27-point penalty

Leics on brink of relegation after points deduction

In its amended decision, the panel said that "in a 162-page bundle prepared by the Cricket Regulator for the tribunal in advance of the original hearing on 12 September, there was no reference by the Cricket Regulator to the County Championship playing conditions and specifically no reference at all to Playing Condition 16.2.6".

It added that its "clear view" was that "eight points is the appropriate deduction and no more".

Confirming it was removing the immediate eight-point sanction, the panel said: "Regrettably that is the limit of this tribunal's powers given that, as both parties agree, it has no power to interfere in any way with the applicability of Playing Condition 16.2.6.

"If it had the power to do so, this tribunal makes it plain that it would have reduced the points deduction to the eight points it imposed in its original decision."

In a statement, , external the Cricket Regulator said: "Following the initial hearing on 11 September and the decision of 15 September, a question arose as to whether the separate 19-point deduction imposed under the Playing Conditions should have been taken into account by the CDP when considering the proportionality of the sanction imposed under the Pitch Regulations.

"In the interests of fairness and transparency, the Cricket Regulator raised this issue with the CDP and Leicestershire CCC. The CDP has now considered this issue and adjusted their decision on the sanction accordingly.

"The amended decision only adjusts the sanction imposed by the CDP in relation to the Pitch Regulations. It does not impact the finding that the charge for a breach of the Pitch Regulations was upheld, and it does not impact the 19-points deduction imposed as a result of the Playing Conditions."

White's statement on Leicestershire's website , external said: "The panel made clear that the latest hearing and amended decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings.

"Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have.

"We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the panel was caused to decide the case."

Both the Cricket Regulator and Leicestershire said it would not comment further while the appeal process is ongoing.

articles.title: County Championship: Leicestershire have eight points reinstated from 27-point deduction for poor pitch blamed on Bollywood film shoot
articles.summary: Leicestershire chief executive Emma White confirms club will still appeal its deduction for the poor pitch that groundsman Callum Lewis later argued was due to a Bollywood film shoot; they will appeal against decision despite having eight points reinstated from original 27-point deduction
articles.body:
The Foxes were relegated from Division One of the County Championship last week following an innings defeat by champions Warwickshire.

Leicestershire's groundsman Callum Lewin had argued filming of an unscheduled Bollywood film - believed to be for a biopic of former India captain Sourav Ganguly - had taken place at the ground four days before the Glamorgan fixture between August 20-23, preventing the pitch from being covered for eight hours in bright sunshine and heatwave temperatures.

The Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) upheld the charge against Leicestershire for a breach of the ECB's Pitch Regulations.

It imposed an immediate eight-point deduction from the County Championship plus the 19 points Leicestershire earned from winning the match by 42 runs.

A further eight-point deduction was also suspended until the end of the 2027 season and a £5,000 fine.

Leicestershire confirmed last Thursday that they would appeal against the original sanction.

Following the CDP holding a further hearing last Wednesday, the sanction has been amended with Leicestershire having eight points reinstated.

Leicestershire chief executive Emma White said in a statement: "The (CDP) Panel made clear that the latest hearing and Amended Decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings.

"Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld, and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have. We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the Panel was caused to decide the case.

"Our recently instructed counsel, Craig Harris, and Oliver Laurence of Periculum Sport shall continue to act for the Club throughout the appeal process.

"As we are now engaged in that process, it would not be appropriate for the club to comment further at this stage. I would again ask all supporters to do the same, and to treat everyone involved, including players and staff from other counties, and those administering this process, with courtesy and respect, both at the ground and online."

The amended decision adjusts Leicestershire's points tally in Division One to 119, 17 behind third-from-bottom Essex.

A wholly successful appeal would lift Leicestershire out of the relegation zone and above Essex.

articles.title: Coaching uncertainty, inadequate preps cloud UP’s Ranji campaign
articles.summary: UP’s Ranji Trophy campaign faces uncertainty as UPCA delays coach appointments and holds limited preseason camp; Gyanendra Pandey leads coaching contenders.
articles.body: Nearly two decades after Uttar Pradesh last won the Ranji Trophy, the state team is again preparing for a new domestic season with uncertainty around its coaching setup and squad finalisation.With less than 12 days left for the start of the senior season, the Uttar Pradesh Cricket Association (UPCA) is yet to announce coaches for the Ranji Trophy side and junior teams.A UPCA source said the Cricket Advisory Committee has prepared a list of recommendations, which will be placed before the association’s annual general meeting.Former India cricketer and former UP Ranji coach Gyanendra Pandey is likely to be the frontrunner for the Ranji Trophy head coach’s role. Current UP selector Rizwan Shamshad and previous edition Ranji trophy coach Arvind Kapoor are also in contention, particularly for white-ball coaching roles.UPCA secretary Prem Manohar Gupta told TOI, “UPCA will announce the appointment of coaches at the annual general meeting on Sept 30.”Uttar Pradesh won its only Ranji Trophy title in 2005-06 under captain Mohammed Kaif and coach Rajinder Singh Hans. The team has finished runner-up five times — in 1939-40, 1977-78, 1997-98, 2007-08 and 2008-09.Pandey had a strong record during his earlier stint with UP in red-ball cricket. Under him, UP reached the Ranji Trophy final in 2007-08 and 2008-09 and made the semi-finals in 2009-10. He was also the coach when UP finished runner-up in the Vijay Hazare Trophy in 2021-22.Shamshad’s coaching record has been prominent in the T20 format. UP won the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy in 2015-16 and finished runner-up in 2013-14 under him. Kapoor, who coached the Ranji side in the previous edition, could not deliver the expected results in red-ball cricket, though UP reached the quarterfinals of the Vijay Hazare Trophy in 2025-26.UP’s record in limited-overs cricket has also been modest. The team has won the Vijay Hazare Trophy once, in 2002-03, and finished runner-up in 2005-06 and 2020-21. In the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, UP won the title in 2015-16 and was runner-up in 2013-14.A senior UPCA official said preparation for the season has been inadequate. “Ahead of the fresh season, UPCA held only one camp of two to three days last week. articles.title: RCA polls narrow to two-way battle as Dhananjai Singh Khimsar, Brij Kishore Upadhyay face off
articles.summary: Jaipur: The race for the Rajasthan Cricket Association (RCA) presidency reached a dramatic crescendo following the withdrawal of nominations on Monday,
articles.body: Jaipur: The race for the Rajasthan Cricket Association (RCA) presidency reached a dramatic crescendo following the withdrawal of nominations on Monday, with the candidate field narrowing down to a high-stakes showdown between Dhananjai Singh Khimsar and Brij Kishore Upadhyay.Electoral officer AK Pande confirmed that 18 nominations were withdrawn out of the 30 initially received, leaving 12 candidates in the fray for six executive posts. With exactly two contenders remaining per seat, straight head-to-head battles have been drawn across the board.RCA insiders suggest the odds currently favour Jodhpur District Cricket Association (DCA) president Khimsar, whose ‘resilience’ and ‘institutional knowledge’ have kept him at the centre of state cricket affairs for years.He was on the verge of claiming the presidency in 2024 before the process was disrupted, and he has maintained a consistent presence on every ad-hoc committee formed to manage RCA operations between 2024 and 2026.However, the opposition is far from subdued. “Upadhyay's (Dausa DCA secretary) entry into the race has injected fresh drama, particularly when he arrived to file his nomination papers accompanied by veteran leader and finance commission chairman Arun Chaturvedi, a prominent figure close to the chief minister, which political insiders suggest indicates govt backing. That said, Khimsar also possesses immense political weight, being the son of the state’s health minister Gajendra Singh Khimsar. Also, let’s not forget that Dhananjai’s extended family shares a strong connection with an influential Central minister,” a source said.Party insiders pointed towards how these elections also bring to light deeper internal factions within the BJP. Earlier, three distinct groups within the party ecosystem were fighting the polls. Following Parakram Singh Rathore’s exit, the contest has condensed into a ‘direct battle between the two remaining camps’.The dynamics of the presidential race have altered now. “Parakram withdrew due to a lack of political support, as he was reportedly running solely on the legacy of his father, former Leader of Opposition Rajendra Singh Rathore, rather than building a broader consensus. And district cricket associations like Bharatpur, Dholpur and Dausa also kept him under the impression that they were in his support, but in reality they were not,” added another source.The competitive spirit extends across the entire ballot, with straight contests shaping up for all executive positions.
